where: Section 3, first sentence of 'Real-time limits matter' (the same claim appears in Quiz Q4 answer)
problem: The text says 'Halting the CPU freezes timers'. Halting the core stops instruction execution, but on most MCUs the on-chip peripherals, timers and watchdog keep counting unless the debugger explicitly sets freeze bits. This is exactly why the chapter's own trap says a halt 'can trigger the watchdog'; the two statements contradict each other, and a student will repeat the wrong one.
fix: Write: 'Halting the CPU stops instruction execution. On most MCUs the timers, serial ports and watchdog keep running unless the debugger freezes them, so interrupts are serviced late and the watchdog can reset the board. In Quiz Q4 answer, say: 'Halting stops instruction execution; the peripherals and watchdog usually keep counting, so the bug that depends on interrupt latency or on the watchdog firing is lost.'

problem: 'it connects to the target socket or a debug header' mixes the two tools. An emulator pod normally plugs into the MCU socket or a dedicated emulation header; reaching the chip through the ordinary debug header is the in-circuit debugger's route, not the emulator's. The chapter has just drawn that distinction and then blurs it.
fix: Write: 'An emulator pod connects to the target socket (or a dedicated emulation header) so that it takes the place of the MCU. An in-circuit debugger, by contrast, needs only the small JTAG or SWD header on the board.'

problem: 'Some syllabi call the on-chip block the debug access port' is loose. The debug access port (DAP) is one specific block inside ARM CoreSight that lets the probe reach memory and peripherals; the whole on-chip debug logic is not called the DAP.
fix: Write: 'In ARM CoreSight chips the block that gives the probe access to the bus and memory is called the debug access port (DAP); the whole on-chip debug logic is usually just called the debug interface.'
